entry.title: A Bayesian Spatially Varying Coefficient Model for Surface Urban Heat Island Estimation

link.title: A Bayesian Spatially Varying Coefficient Model for Surface Urban Heat Island Estimation

entry.content:
Surface urban heat islands (SUHIs) are commonly studied using satellite-derived land surface temperature (LST), but many analyses rely on static summaries or pointwise urban-rural contrasts, providing limited inference on temporal change, spatial dependence, and uncertainty. This study models LST as a stochastic spatio-temporal process using a spatially varying coefficient formulation that decomposes LST into a baseline spatial field and a location-specific temporal trend. This structure allows persistent thermal differences and local warming rates to be estimated within a unified probabilistic framework. SUHI is derived from the posterior distribution of the baseline spatial field by contrasting the estimated LST at a given pixel with the minimum estimated LST among non-urban pixels. Posterior excursion probabilities are used to identify areas where temporal changes are supported under simultaneous probability control. The framework is applied to summer Landsat 8 LST observations for Bologna, Italy, from 2013 to 2025. Results show strong spatial heterogeneity in SUHI, with higher values over impervious surfaces and lower values over forests and water bodies. Summer LST increased overall, but local trends varied markedly across the municipality. Joint excursion sets identify areas with warming greater than the domain-wide average and smaller clusters with statistically supported cooling. These results reveal changing thermal patterns across Bologna and help distinguish areas experiencing increasing surface heat from locations where thermal conditions have improved over time. The framework therefore provides an uncertainty-aware basis for monitoring urban thermal change.

entry.title: A Bayesian hierarchical push-forward method for cluster Randomized Controlled Trial power calculations in complex humanitarian settings

link.title: A Bayesian hierarchical push-forward method for cluster Randomized Controlled Trial power calculations in complex humanitarian settings

entry.content:
The design and evaluation of public health interventions in humanitarian crises demand rigorous yet flexible methodological approaches. Cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) are increasingly used to generate evidence in such settings, but trial conduct is frequently complicated by displacement, resource constraints, and cluster dropout. Although Bayesian methods provide a natural framework for hierarchical modeling, probabilistic uncertainty quantification, and the integration of prior knowledge, their use in cRCT design remains limited, particularly with respect to anticipating missingness. This paper introduces a Bayesian design strategy tailored for cRCTs in complex settings, motivated by a forthcoming trial in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, that will assess a community health worker adherence intervention for cardiovascular disease and hepatitis C. Our approach incorporates prior information on cluster and individual-level dropout into power and sample size calculations via a hierarchical model and push-forward distribution framework. Through simulation studies, we evaluate the performance of the proposed method under varying levels of missingness and correlation structures. The approach is then applied to inform the design of the Bangladesh trial. We disseminate our methods via a publicly-available R Shiny app to promote accessibility and usability to investigators. By formalizing Bayesian strategies that anticipate data loss, this work provides a foundation for more robust and efficient cRCTs in humanitarian contexts; therefore, strengthening the evidence base for health interventions in resource-limited and crisis-affected populations.

entry.title: A Distribution-to-Distribution Neural Probabilistic Forecasting Framework for Dynamical Systems

link.title: A Distribution-to-Distribution Neural Probabilistic Forecasting Framework for Dynamical Systems

entry.content:
Probabilistic forecasts provide a principled representation of forecast uncertainty through predictive distributions. Directly propagating predictive distributions with conventional physical models requires solving distributional evolution equations, a task well-known to be computationally prohibitive for high-dimensional nonlinear systems. Consequently, multi-step predictive distributions are commonly approximated using ensembles or sampled trajectories. A novel distribution-to-distribution (D2D) neural probabilistic forecasting framework is proposed with compatible distributional encoding and decoding interfaces around a replaceable neural forecasting module. Kernel mean embeddings represent input distributions, while mixture density networks parameterise outputs, enabling recursive multi-step forecasting in distributional form. The framework is demonstrated on the Lorenz63 system. Results show that the D2D model captures nontrivial distributional evolution, produces skillful probabilistic forecasts without explicit ensemble simulation, and remains competitive with a naively initialised perfect-model benchmark. This provides proof-of-concept evidence that predictive distributions can be recursively propagated through a neural forecasting model and evaluated in terms of probabilistic forecast performance.

entry.title: A Geometric Framework for the Bayesian Estimation of Joint Environmental Extremes

link.title: A Geometric Framework for the Bayesian Estimation of Joint Environmental Extremes

entry.content:
Multivariate extreme events tend to have broader impacts on society compared to individual extremes. Flexible and accurate modeling of multivariate extremes is therefore crucial for many practical applications, including risk assessments and mitigation projects. In this work, we introduce a Bayesian modeling framework for bivariate extremes. Our approach utilizes the geometric extremes framework, for which data are decomposed into angular and radial components. The angular distribution is estimated using periodic M-splines, resulting in a natural circular density, while the radial distribution, conditional on the angles, is approximated using Bezier splines. The radial distribution also provides a means of estimating the limit set, the limiting shape of scaled sample clouds that encodes information pertaining to extremal dependence. Our Bayesian approach offers advantages over competing methods, particularly for uncertainty quantification and interpretation. Furthermore, our framework guarantees theoretical properties of limit sets, ensuring validity for inference. Notably, our model can be used to approximate extreme probabilities associated with failure sets in the joint tail, which are useful across many applications. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through numerical experiments and a case study on fire weather in Louisiana, USA, with diagnostics for the latter indicating strong model performance.

entry.title: A Greedy PDE Router for Blending Neural Operators and Classical Methods

link.title: A Greedy PDE Router for Blending Neural Operators and Classical Methods

entry.content:
When solving PDEs, classical numerical solvers are often computationally expensive, while machine learning methods can suffer from spectral bias, failing to capture high-frequency components. Designing an optimal hybrid iterative solver–where, at each iteration, a solver is selected from an ensemble of solvers to leverage their complementary strengths–poses a challenging combinatorial problem. While greedy selection is desirable for its constant-factor approximation guarantee to the optimal solution under Lipschitz assumptions, it requires knowledge of the true error at each step, which is unavailable in practice. We address this by proposing an approximate greedy router that efficiently mimics a greedy approach to solver selection. Empirical results on the Poisson, convection-diffusion, and anisotropic diffusion equations show that our method consistently reduces time-to-solution relative to single-solver baselines and existing hybrid approaches such as HINTS.

entry.title: A Latent-Space Statistical Learning Framework for Semicontinuous Outcomes: Regularized Deviance and Boundary-Stabilized Optimization

link.title: A Latent-Space Statistical Learning Framework for Semicontinuous Outcomes: Regularized Deviance and Boundary-Stabilized Optimization

entry.content:
Semicontinuous outcomes characterized by an exact zero mass and heavy-tailed continuous distributions challenge empirical risk modeling and machine learning. Compound Poisson-Gamma Tweedie processes impose a rigid mean-variance coupling that distorts zero-mass probabilities under extreme tail dispersion, flattening continuous density and reducing extreme-risk discrimination. Furthermore, heuristic post-hoc target capping introduces systematic bias while leaving loss gradients vulnerable to tail leverage. We present a unified, statistically coherent likelihood framework for semicontinuous modeling under arbitrary zero-inflation and explicit upper boundary constraints. Optimization and likelihood evaluations operate strictly in a latent space defined by the power-scaling mapping $y_i^* = \min{(y_i/s)^\lambda, U^*}$, where $s \in (0, U)$ anchors scale and $\lambda \in (0,1)$ regularizes tail curvature. The architecture partitions the response into three regimes: an unconstrained Bernoulli hurdle, an analytical continuous Gamma body, and an upper boundary point mass governed by incomplete Gamma survival ratios. Rather than an arbitrary truncation, the boundary functions as an intrinsic tail accumulator bounding score and Hessian dynamics. We derive the closed-form deviance objective, score vectors, and block-diagonal Hessian matrix, proving that parameter spaces are information-orthogonal to enable concurrent classification and regression updates. Asymptotic boundary analysis demonstrates that score and curvature scale linearly in the deep tail, establishing a quadratic restoring force that prevents gradient collapse. The framework breaks the Tweedie parameter rigidity paradox while maintaining structural fidelity across both zero occurrence and extreme severity differentiation.

entry.title: A Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Multi-Stream Quickest Change Detection

link.title: A Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Multi-Stream Quickest Change Detection

entry.content:
A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework is proposed for quickest change detection (QCD) where there are multiple experts, and each expert produces a sequence of statistics for change detection. A change is declared when a weighted sum of these statistics crosses a threshold. This framework is then applied to the problem of multi-stream QCD to obtain a family of powerful algorithms that outperform the best known algorithms in the literature. In the multi-stream QCD problem, a decision-maker observes multiple streams of observations. At the change point, the distribution of an unknown subset of the streams changes. The optimal algorithm based on a generalized likelihood ratio is computationally expensive. One of the most computationally and performance-efficient algorithms in the literature is the rank-weighted sum (RWS) scheme based on Shiryaev-Roberts statistics. It is shown in the paper that the MoE-based QCD algorithm for multi-stream data outperforms the RWS scheme. This is demonstrated through simulation results on real-valued Gaussian mean shift data and high-dimensional data from Gaussian–Bernoulli Restricted Boltzmann Machines (GB-RBMs).

link.title: A Model Ensemble-Based Post-Processing Framework for Fairness-Aware Prediction

entry.content:
Striking an optimal balance between predictive performance and fairness continues to be a fundamental challenge in machine learning. In this work, we propose a post-processing framework that facilitates fairness-aware prediction by leveraging model ensembling. Designed to operate independently of any specific model internals, our approach is widely applicable across various learning tasks, model architectures, and fairness definitions. Through extensive experiments spanning classification, regression, and survival analysis, we demonstrate that the framework effectively enhances fairness while maintaining, or only minimally affecting, predictive accuracy.

entry.title: A One-Sided McDiarmid-Type Inequality for Heavy Tails via Reverse KL Tensorization

link.title: A One-Sided McDiarmid-Type Inequality for Heavy Tails via Reverse KL Tensorization

entry.content:
We revisit McDiarmid’s inequality, a central tool in statistical learning theory and algorithm analysis. We show that large deviations above the mean are exponentially unlikely for functions of independent random variables that are almost surely bounded above and satisfy a conditional moment assumption of order $p\in(1,2]$. When $p<2$, the result applies even when the function has infinite variance. Our proof relies on a new tensorization inequality for the Kullback–Leibler divergence, termed reverse KL tensorization, which may be of independent interest. Applications include concentration of the sample mean and median-of-means estimator, and one-sided uniform risk bounds for unbounded losses.

entry.title: Acceleration and its Limits in Gaussian Variational Inference

link.title: Acceleration and its Limits in Gaussian Variational Inference

entry.content:
We study whether the classical momentum-based acceleration that improves the condition-number dependence of gradient descent from $\kappa$ to $\sqrt{\kappa}$ for strongly convex, smooth objectives extends to Gaussian variational inference (GVI) for strongly log-concave, log-smooth target distributions. With exact Gaussian expectations, a convex composite formulation of GVI yields the classical accelerated $\sqrt{\kappa}$ convergence rate. However, when only pointwise derivatives are available, we construct a family of strongly log-concave targets for which any randomized algorithm requires $\kappa^{1-o(1)}$ queries to achieve a fixed objective accuracy, even when the initial objective gap is bounded independently of $\kappa$. Thus curvature bounds alone cannot guarantee uniform accelerated total-query complexity. We then ask which additional structure permits acceleration and give positive examples: under a Hessian-Lipschitz assumption, variance-reduced stochastic methods yield accelerated guarantees when the Hessian variation is sufficiently small. Finally, experiments on real datasets show substantial empirical speedups from acceleration across a broad range of methods.

entry.title: Accuracy of Uniform Inference on Fine Grid Points

link.title: Accuracy of Uniform Inference on Fine Grid Points

entry.content:
Uniform confidence bands are widely used in empirical analysis for uncertainty qualification of nonparametric inference of unknown functions. A variety of simple implementation methods, including multiplier bootstrap, have been proposed and theoretically justified. However, an implementation over a literally continuous index set is generally computationally infeasible, and practitioners therefore compute the critical value by evaluating the statistic on a finite evaluation grid. This paper quantifies the effect of this discretization on coverage accuracy and investigates how fine the evaluation grid must be to ensure valid uniform inference. We first illustrate through simulations of a kernel-based nonparametric estimator that coarse grids can invalidate uniform inference. Surprisingly, increasing the sample size can worsen coverage on a fixed coarse grid, even as the remaining approximation error on the grid decreases. We then derive general upper bounds on the coverage probability and coverage error of uniform confidence bands based on finite-grid multiplier-bootstrap critical values. These bounds distinguish discretization error from the remaining approximation error on the grid. For local empirical processes arising from kernel smoothing, we further establish primitive conditions under which coverage converges to zero, even when the number of grid points diverges, and conditions under which asymptotically nominal coverage is attained. These results yield rate-sharp grid resolution requirements in terms of the bandwidth.

entry.title: A perturbation theory for Feynman-Kac models and their particle interpretations

link.title: A perturbation theory for Feynman-Kac models and their particle interpretations

entry.content:
We develop a perturbation analysis of Feynman–Kac models, describing how local errors introduced at each step of the Feynman–Kac recursion propagate over time. Under general conditions on the potential functions and the Markov transitions, which are shown to hold for a large class of state-space models, we prove that the global error for any time horizon $T\geq 1$ is bounded by $C\,\Delta_T\log(1+\Delta_T^{-1})$, where $\Delta_T$ is the largest local error; this bound holds both for the prediction and the updated models. These conditions require no Lyapunov function and no stability of the Markov transitions, and allow for non-compact state spaces: confinement is provided by the potential functions. Our perturbation bounds hold in total variation and in the Kolmogorov norm; for the latter, we extend the Hardy–Krause variation and the Koksma–Hlawka inequality to unbounded domains. Our perturbation theory is applied to derive time-uniform bounds for linearized Kalman filters, Euler schemes for partially observed diffusions and nudged state-space models, as well as high-probability error bounds, uniform over whole trajectories, for particle filters and, more generally, for mean field particle methods such as sequential Monte Carlo and diffusion Monte Carlo algorithms.

entry.title: A proximal gradient algorithm for composite log-concave sampling

link.title: A proximal gradient algorithm for composite log-concave sampling

entry.content:
We propose an algorithm to sample from composite log-concave distributions over $\mathbb{R}^d$, i.e., densities of the form $\pi\propto e^{-f-g}$, assuming access to gradient evaluations of $\alpha_f$-convex $f$ and a restricted Gaussian oracle (RGO) for $\alpha_g$-convex $g$, where $\alpha_g \ge 0$. The latter requirement means that we can easily sample from the density $\text{RGO}_{g,h,y}(x) \propto \exp(-g(x) -\frac{1}{2h}   y-x   ^2)$, which is the sampling analogue of the proximal operator for $g$. If $f + g$ is $\alpha$-convex and $f$ is $\beta$-smooth, our sampler achieves $\varepsilon$ error in total variation distance using $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\kappa \sqrt d \log^4(1/\varepsilon))$ oracle calls where $\kappa := 1 \vee \beta/\alpha$, with $0\le \alpha_g \le \beta$ and $\alpha := \alpha_f + \alpha_g > 0$, which matches prior state-of-the-art results for the case $g=0$. We further extend our results to cases where (1) $\pi$ is non-log-concave but satisfies a Poincar'e or log-Sobolev inequality, and (2) $f$ is non-smooth but Lipschitz.

entry.title: Are continuous models better than areal models for spatial disease mapping with a large number of small areas?

link.title: Are continuous models better than areal models for spatial disease mapping with a large number of small areas?

entry.content:
Classical methods for analysing areal mortality data typically rely on Poisson mixed models, which account for spatial and unstructured variability through prior distributions such as the BYM2 prior. This paper investigates alternative modeling approaches for settings involving a large number of small areas. Specifically, we explore the Stochastic Partial Differential Equation (SPDE) approach for continuous risk surfaces, examining an existing model from the literature alongside a proposed modification that incorporates an unstructured random effect. Finally, we evaluate the performance of both hierarchical mixed Poisson models and SPDE-based frameworks through a comprehensive simulation study across various spatial configurations and aggregation levels. Furthermore, we apply these approaches to the analysis of lung cancer mortality among men and women across Spanish municipalities during the period 2009–2022.

entry.title: Asymmetric Space-Time Covariance Functions via Hierarchical Mixtures

link.title: Asymmetric Space-Time Covariance Functions via Hierarchical Mixtures

entry.content:
This work is focused on constructing space-time covariance functions through a hierarchical mixture approach that can serve as building blocks for capturing complex dependency structures. This approach provides a unifying modeling framework that not only constructs a new class of asymmetric space-time covariance functions with closed-form expressions, but also provides corresponding space-time process representations, which further unify constructions for several existing space-time covariance models. This hierarchical mixture framework decomposes the complexity of model specification at different levels of hierarchy, for which parsimonious covariance models can be specified with simple mixing measures to yield flexible properties and closed forms. A characterization theorem is provided to study how the mixing measures determine the statistical properties of covariance functions. Several new covariance models resulting from this framework are discussed in terms of their practical usefulness. This hierarchical mixture approach is extended for nonstationary and multivariate settings. A theorem is also provided to construct valid asymmetric space-time covariance functions with arbitrary and possibly different degrees of smoothness and long-range dependence in space and in time. This generalized class also bridges a theoretical gap in using the Lagrangian reference framework. The superior performance of several new parsimonious covariance models over existing models is verified with the well-known Irish wind data and the U.S. air temperature data.

entry.title: Bayesian Adaptive Tensor Smoothing for Multiway Demographic Counts

link.title: Bayesian Adaptive Tensor Smoothing for Multiway Demographic Counts

entry.content:
Demographic data are often collected across multiple dimensions such as time, age, subnational region, and sex. Modeling such data is challenging due to the interplay of high dimensionality, heterogeneity between groups, and stochastic variability within small groups. This paper proposes a Bayesian adaptive tensor smoothing model for multiway demographic counts that represents the latent log-rate array as a sum of rank-one components. Global-local shrinkage priors control the effective rank of the decomposition, the number of modes along which each component varies, and the smoothness that Gaussian process priors impose along ordered modes such as age and time. Posterior inference relies on a data augmentation Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm that interweaves centered and noncentered parameterizations in every layer of the model to keep mixing satisfactory in large and sparse count arrays. Applied to Swedish county-level and sex-specific mortality from 1969 to 2024, the model recovers stable demographic surfaces and life table quantities from noisy small-population data. In cross-validation exercises, the method outperforms both canonical demographic benchmarks and existing count tensor factorizations.

entry.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Longitudinal Factor Model for Microbiome Counts

link.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Longitudinal Factor Model for Microbiome Counts

entry.content:
Longitudinal microbiome studies provide important insights into the temporal evolution of microbial abundances and dynamic cross-feature dependence. Modeling longitudinal microbiome data is challenging because microbiome counts are highly heterogeneous and zero-inflated, and, moreover, repeated measurements induce within-subject temporal dependence and possibly time-varying cross-feature covariance. To address these challenges, we develop a flexible Bayesian longitudinal factor model using a rounded log-normal latent representation. The mean abundance process begins with a Dirichlet process mixture baseline, which accommodates sparse and multimodal abundance distributions, and subsequently evolves through an autoregressive process. Autoregressive coefficients differ across prespecified biological groups, which are defined by genotypes in our application. A separate autoregressive factor process captures shared cross-feature dependence. The model therefore distinguishes subject–feature mean evolution from shared dependence and yields a closed-form, time-indexed covariance. Simulation studies evaluate dynamic covariance recovery under matched and misspecified data-generating mechanisms. In the longitudinal mouse-gut microbiome application, LODI identifies highly persistent feature-specific abundance trajectories and shared latent factors that distinguish the three genotype groups over time. At week 15, the dominant factor follows the observed WT < ACK/G < HACK/G tumor-severity ordering, with its strongest contributions arising from OTUs classified within Clostridiaceae, Clostridium, and RF39.

entry.title: Benchmarking Priors: A Fully Bayesian Approach to Small Area Benchmarking

link.title: Benchmarking Priors: A Fully Bayesian Approach to Small Area Benchmarking

entry.content:
We develop a new class of priors for Bayesian small area models under strict external bench- marking constraints. The prior is fully supported on the constrained parameter set defined by the benchmarking constraints and thereby provides a proper constrained posterior that is fully supported on the restricted set. The posterior naturally constrains the small area estimates to conform to the benchmarking values at the aggregate level. In addition, it facilitates valid uncertainty quantification using credible sets that are fully contained within the constrained set. This novel framework has a wide range of applicability, ranging from the standard Gaus- sian Fay-Herriot model to more general Fay-Herriot models, such as robust Fay-Herriot models, where the area-level random effects are distributed as multivariate t, or Fay-Herriot models where there is a complex nonlinear relationship between the area means and the covariates. The numerical results reaffirm the advantages of the proposed benchmarking priors.

entry.title: Beyond Match Results: Bayesian Mediation of Ability, Performance, and Winning in Professional Tennis

link.title: Beyond Match Results: Bayesian Mediation of Ability, Performance, and Winning in Professional Tennis

entry.content:
Match results measure competitive ability, but they do not explain how ability is expressed during play. Match statistics offer a natural mediator, however performance is usually measured over the same match as the outcome: a full-match statistic uses events that help determine the winner, while a first-set statistic is earlier but rests on fewer service points and still contributes to the result. Comparing the two therefore mixes timing and precision. We develop a Bayesian mediation framework for this problem. Dynamic abilities on hard, clay, and grass courts are estimated from previous seasons only and are linked to both players’ service performance, and a Bradley–Terry model relates ability and performance to the match result. A control mediator samples the first set’s number of service points from the full match, separating the measurement window from the point count. In 3,820 men’s matches, the hard-court mediated share rises from 0.52 with a first-set mediator to 0.95 with a full-match mediator; the point-count contrast accounts for 0.30 of this gap and the window contrast for 0.13. The pattern replicates on the women’s tour. Simulations and sensitivity analyzes examine the decomposition and assumptions needed for a causal interpretation.

entry.title: Boltzmann generators for amorphous particle systems

link.title: Boltzmann generators for amorphous particle systems

entry.content:
Sampling configurations in thermodynamic equilibrium is a long-standing challenge in statistical physics. Boltzmann generators address this problem by employing generative models to propose independent configurations, which are then reweighted via importance sampling using exact likelihood evaluations. Recent Boltzmann Generators based on continuous normalizing flows and flow matching have achieved significant success for particle systems and biomolecules. However, these approaches have not been extended to amorphous materials (glasses), for which equilibrium sampling is notoriously slow. Because of their disordered structure, the invariances and geometrical constraints of amorphous materials differ from those of crystals and biomolecules, preventing the direct use of existing generative models. Here, we develop Boltzmann Generators tailored to amorphous materials by building the required equivariances directly into Riemannian stochastic interpolants. Our framework incorporates periodic boundary conditions and particle symmetries using equivariant graph neural networks. Numerical experiments demonstrate that enforcing physical symmetries significantly improves the accuracy of Boltzmann Generators, but also reveal an intrinsic limitation of the continuous-flow formulation: accumulated numerical errors during likelihood integration break time-reversibility, compromising exact thermodynamic reweighting. These results reveal a fundamental challenge for continuous-flow generative models in statistical mechanics and call for alternative approaches that preserve exact thermodynamic consistency.

entry.title: Boundary inference for the Makeham term in mortality models

link.title: Boundary inference for the Makeham term in mortality models

entry.content:
Whether a mortality model needs a Makeham term, the constant representing background mortality, is commonly decided with a likelihood-ratio test. The constant cannot be negative, so testing its absence places it on a boundary, where the usual chi-squared calibration fails. Assuming independent Poisson death counts and standard regularity conditions, we show that when the constant is the only parameter on a boundary the statistic converges to an equal mixture of a point mass at zero and a chi-squared distribution with one degree of freedom: at the 5% level the critical value is 2.71, not 3.84. We state conditions under which the correction holds for Makeham models, verify them for Gompertz–Makeham and gamma-Gompertz–Makeham, and quantify the information about the constant, which fixes the local power, the smallest detectable term, and the loss of detectability as the age window narrows. When a gamma-frailty variance is estimated at a true value of zero, the limit is no longer a chi-squared mixture and the correction rejects too often. Monte Carlo experiments show the conventional cutoff rejecting at half the nominal level, a correctly calibrated test missing a term at its detection threshold in most samples, and excess rejections persisting as exposure grows.

link.title: Calibrated Bayesian inference for overall and subgroup-specific causal effects in stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trials

entry.content:
Stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trials (SW-CRTs) randomly assign clusters to sequences that determine when each cluster switches from control to intervention. Conventional Bayesian analyses of SW-CRTs report treatment effect coefficients from a working outcome model, but under model misspecification or informative cluster-period sizes, such coefficients can lack a clear causal interpretation. In this work, we develop Bayesian methods targeting weighted average treatment effect estimands in SW-CRTs, including novel subgroup-specific causal estimands defined by baseline characteristics. We compare model-based g-computation with model-robust standardization, implementing both with linear mixed models and mixed-effects Bayesian additive regression trees as working outcome models, and propose a calibrated variance estimator that augments posterior parameter uncertainty with cluster-level resampling to better capture sampling variability. In simulations with outcome model misspecification and informative cluster-period sizes, model-robust standardization with calibrated inference exhibits negligible bias and near-nominal frequentist coverage for overall and subgroup-specific causal effects, whereas g-computation and uncalibrated intervals become insufficient. We illustrate the proposed methods with a reanalysis of the Trauma Survivors Outcomes and Support trial.

entry.title: Calibrated Transfer Learning for Survival Prediction and Treatment Inference

link.title: Calibrated Transfer Learning for Survival Prediction and Treatment Inference

entry.content:
Historical survival data can improve prediction in a cohort with few events, but prognostic differences can make borrowing harmful. To borrow while adapting, we propose calibrated transfer learning for the Cox model, in which a historical risk function enters the target analysis as a fixed offset with a prespecified correction for changing covariate effects and a separate baseline hazard. Calibration removes historical error in the correction space exactly, so only the remaining error governs the prediction rate, for any bounded learner. Accurate prediction does not, however, ensure valid treatment inference. In randomized trials, the remaining error biases the conditional treatment coefficient, because a treatment effect changes the prognostic composition of later risk sets. We characterize this bias and its sharp worst-case direction, and we introduce a cross-fitted projected score that removes it at first order and leaves only a second-order bias when a fixed error lies in its dictionary. A historical learning bound separates approximation, sampling, and optimization error. In simulations, calibration improves prediction when the historical risk is well learned, and the projected score restores interval coverage under drift outside the correction, also at a hazard ratio of 0.7. In a retrospective transfer between the POPLAR and OAK lung cancer trials, selected corrections reduce the integrated Brier score by 4.3\% relative to ridge-penalized clinical Cox with 100 training patients, without improving treatment precision.

entry.title: Causal Fingerprints Reveal Hidden Mechanisms in Partially-Observed Dynamical Systems

link.title: Causal Fingerprints Reveal Hidden Mechanisms in Partially-Observed Dynamical Systems

entry.content:
In partially-observed dynamical systems, distinct hidden mechanisms can produce similar observable summary statistics while explaining individual events differently. We introduce causal fingerprints: realization-dependent patterns that track how information about a hidden state is revealed through subsequent evolution. Within a prescribed dynamical model, we compare the filtering posterior, based on observations up to a given time, with the smoothing posterior, obtained after adding an expanding window of future observations. We quantify this retrospective information gain using Kullback-Leibler divergence and track its evolution as the future window of observational data expands. The fingerprint reveals both the strength and temporal reach of hidden influence, which can vary across events and their stages. Because the observed trajectory is held fixed while hidden-state inference depends on the candidate model, fingerprints reveal how competing dynamical mechanisms explain the same observations even when selected statistics agree. In linear Gaussian systems, we derive a characteristic fingerprint timescale for the temporal reach of hidden influence. Calibrated surrogates matching the observable mean, variance, and decorrelation time can still produce distinct fingerprints when feedback memory, hidden-noise memory, or hidden forcing timescales are misrepresented. Nonlinear examples reveal mechanism-dependent signatures for extreme bursts, oscillatory variability, and regime switching, including multiplicative instability versus additive forcing, deterministic nonlinear feedback versus state-dependent multiplicative noise, and intrinsic bistability versus hidden double-well forcing. Causal fingerprints therefore provide a time- and event-resolved diagnostic for asking not only whether a model reproduces observed statistics, but how its hidden dynamics explain individual events.

link.title: Causal Mediation Analysis for Panel Data with Double/Debiased Machine Learning

entry.content:
We develop a double/debiased machine learning framework for causal mediation analysis in panel data with two-way fixed effects. Binary, multivalued, or continuous treatments and continuous mediators affect outcomes via histories. We formulate partially linear models for potential outcomes and mediators, define history-specific direct, indirect, and total effects, and identify them under a sequential conditional independence assumption given unit effects, allowing arbitrary time-invariant confounding. Estimation combines first-differencing, cross-fitting sample splitting that removes period effects, and machine-learned confounding functions within a GMM framework whose score is Neyman orthogonal in all nuisance components. We establish asymptotic normality of the estimators for the structural parameters and causal estimands and provide consistent variance estimators. Simulations show small bias and near-nominal coverage under nonlinear confounding, whereas a DML-free benchmark fails severely for indirect effects. An application to U.S. county data illustrates that a stable total effect can conceal substantial sensitivity in its direct-indirect decomposition.

entry.title: Classical methods for modern applications: synthetic tabular data generation using lightweight discrete response continuous latent variable model

link.title: Classical methods for modern applications: synthetic tabular data generation using lightweight discrete response continuous latent variable model

entry.content:
In this paper, we present a lightweight algorithm for modelling tabular data containing both continuous and discrete variables. The method uses empirical marginal distributions and a selected quantile function to transform the data into a continuous latent space, where a distribution of choice, e.g. a multivariate Gaussian, can be efficiently estimated and applied. While this approach is closely related to classical well-established machine learning methods, we present a novel adaptation that fits well within the contemporary computational ecosystem. Unlike in the case of deep architectures, it results in a simple implementation with few dependencies, robust training/estimation, as well as efficient sampling. The transformation preserves complex marginal distributions and correlations, providing high-fidelity models, especially for data with unimodal distributions. One of the key characteristics of the proposed approach is its continuous representation of discrete variables. While highly desirable, this introduces a significant challenge, since a single observation corresponds to a region rather than a point in the latent space. We show that this ambiguity naturally leads to a Monte Carlo expectation-maximisation (MCEM) formulation, whose auxiliary objective can be expressed as a weighted latent-space likelihood. This, in turn, allows conventional maximum-likelihood estimators to be used within an efficient and robust optimisation procedure.

link.title: CleanRM: Reward Modeling from Noisy Feedback with a Few Clean Feedback for RLHF

entry.content:
Feedback noise is pervasive in preference data, arising from subjective human judgments, annotation mistakes, and imperfect LLM judges. Standard reward modeling trained on such feedback yields a biased estimate of the clean risk. Although classical denoising methods are directly applicable to noisy feedback learning, they generally assume a uniform noise ratio across samples. However, this assumption fails for feedback data, where noise is intrinsically sample-wise. To address this challenge, we propose CleanRM, which uses a few clean feedback to calibrate sample-wise noise ratios via optimal transport. entry.title: Clinically Interpretable Biological Age Estimation Using CatBoost and SHAP with Continuous and Categorical Features from NHANES

link.title: Clinically Interpretable Biological Age Estimation Using CatBoost and SHAP with Continuous and Categorical Features from NHANES

entry.content:
Biological age (BA) captures inter-individual variation in physiological aging beyond chronological age (CA). Although machine-learning models have advanced BA estimation, many rely primarily on continuous laboratory biomarkers, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) dependence plots are typically interpreted visually. We developed a clinically interpretable machine-learning framework for BA estimation using heterogeneous clinical data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES 2011-March 2020, N = 24,983 adults aged >= 18). A CatBoost regression model incorporated 44 demographic, laboratory, physical examination, and lifestyle predictors to estimate CA, defining model-estimated age as BA. SHAP provided multi-level interpretability. Crucially, building on standard visual inspection, we implemented a prespecified automated procedure directly on SHAP dependence plots to quantify feature-value ranges associated with lowest and highest BA contributions, corresponding adjustment magnitudes, and zero-crossing thresholds. Model-estimated BA strongly correlated with CA in held-out testing data (Pearson r = 0.798, P < 0.001). Population-level SHAP identified blood urea nitrogen, serum glucose, vigorous recreational activity, red cell distribution width, and alanine aminotransferase among the leading predictors, with three categorical variables ranking among the top 25. Automated quantitative SHAP analysis mapped predictor-specific ranges, effect sizes, and inflection points, while waterfall plots enabled individual explanations. By extending qualitative visual interpretation to reproducible quantitative metrics across heterogeneous clinical data, this framework enhances transparency and provides a scalable methodological foundation for biological aging research and precision health.

entry.title: Clustering extremal dependence structures via Wasserstein distances between angular measures

link.title: Clustering extremal dependence structures via Wasserstein distances between angular measures

entry.content:
Compound extreme events cause damage out of proportion to their frequency, and grouping random vectors by their joint extremal behaviour is a recurring task in climate science, hydrology, and finance. Classical clustering is driven by typical observations, while existing extremal procedures either summarize dependence by a single coefficient or discretize the simplex in an ad hoc way. We propose a dissimilarity that compares complete angular measures by optimal transport: each angular measure is estimated above a high radial threshold, mapped from the simplex into a Euclidean space of Aitchison coordinates, and compared by the 1-Wasserstein distance. The methodology is fully nonparametric and requires no fitted model. The dissimilarities feed any distance-based clustering algorithm. Under intermediate-threshold asymptotics and mild moment and separation conditions, hierarchical clustering and partitioning around medoids based on them recovers the latent partition with probability tending to one. In simulations, the proposed approach matches established competitors when clusters differ mainly in the strength of extremal dependence and performs substantially better when equal-strength clusters differ in the shape of their angular measures, especially when asymmetry drives the separation. Applications to rain–snowmelt–runoff extremes in Swiss catchments and to extremal co-movement between international equity markets and the US market reveal hydrologically and economically interpretable groups.

entry.title: CoCopula: Conformal Calibration and Copula Aggregation for Reliable Renewable Energy Forecasting

link.title: CoCopula: Conformal Calibration and Copula Aggregation for Reliable Renewable Energy Forecasting

entry.content:
The rapid growth of renewable energy penetration has intensified the need for reliable probabilistic forecasts to support grid operations at aggregated (fleet or system) levels. In practice, however, system operators often lack access to fleet-level probabilistic models and instead rely on site-level forecasts produced by heterogeneous third-party providers. Constructing coherent and calibrated fleet-level probabilistic forecasts from such inputs remains challenging due to complex cross-site dependencies and aggregation-induced miscalibration. Motivated by a real-world operational challenge identified through collaboration with an industry partner, this paper presents a probabilistic aggregation and calibration framework that directly converts site-level probabilistic forecasts into reliable fleet-level forecasts. The paper introduces \method~ (\textbf{Co}nformal Calibration and \textbf{Copula} Aggregation), which integrates Copula-based dependence modeling to capture cross-site correlations followed by Context-Aware Conformal Prediction (CACP) to mitigate miscalibration at the aggregated level. This combination enables dependence-aware aggregation while improving empirical coverage and maintaining sharp prediction intervals. Experiments on large-scale solar generation datasets from three system operators in the United States including MISO, ERCOT, and SPP demonstrate that the proposed \method{} approach achieves near-nominal empirical coverage and consistently lower Winkler scores than competing aggregation-based baselines across different target coverage levels. Importantly, \method{} achieves performance comparable to directly calibrated system-level forecasts, demonstrating its practical value when dedicated fleet-level forecasting models are unavailable.

entry.title: Comparison of Bayesian methods for extrapolation of treatment effects: a simulation study

link.title: Comparison of Bayesian methods for extrapolation of treatment effects: a simulation study

entry.content:
Extrapolating treatment effects from related studies is a promising strategy for designing and analyzing clinical trials in situations where achieving an adequate sample size is challenging. Bayesian methods are well-suited for this purpose, as they enable the synthesis of prior information through the use of prior distributions. While the operating characteristics of Bayesian approaches for borrowing data from control arms have been extensively studied, methods that borrow treatment effects–quantities derived from the comparison between two arms–remain less well understood. In this paper, we present the findings of an extensive simulation study designed to address this gap, across six clinically motivated case studies covering continuous, binary, recurrent-event, and time-to-event endpoints. We varied target sample size, treatment-effect drift, and endpoint-specific design assumptions. Power and estimation performance were compared using a frequentist analysis of the target data alone, calibrated to the same actual type I error rate. Our results provide insights into the strengths and limitations of existing methods in the context of confirmatory trials. At matched actual type I error rates, power differences were usually small, with occasional gains over the reference analysis and larger losses for some adaptive procedures. Borrowing reduced MSE when source and target effects were consistent, but increasing drift eroded this benefit and could substantially reduce interval coverage. Commensurate priors with appropriately chosen hyperpriors offered the most favorable balance between estimation gains and robustness to conflict. The conditional power prior was competitive for estimation at comparable type I error rates, despite its lack of adaptation. Test-then-pool procedures often performed poorly. No method dominated across all criteria.

entry.title: Complete or Sparse: A Tale of Two Identifiabilities

link.title: Complete or Sparse: A Tale of Two Identifiabilities

entry.content:
Understanding when neural networks learn interpretable representations is central to mechanistic interpretability. We study this through identifiability: when can supervised learning recover the true latent variables underlying the data? We introduce two data generating processes distinguished by their causal direction where either labels cause latents (generative) or latents cause labels (discriminative). When the representation has at least as many dimensions as the latent space, we prove that the optimal encoders are linear in the latents. Conversely, when dimensions are insufficient, identifiability generically fails and encoders become nonlinear. We then show that additional constraints yield recovery of individual latent variables, not just linear mixtures. In the generative setting, non-negative activations and energy efficiency force each neuron to encode exactly one latent, providing a precise account of selective grandmother cell-like responses. In the discriminative setting, when latents are sparse and the true measurement matrix satisfies the spark condition, the learned encoder inherits compressed sensing structure, enabling sparse dictionary learning to perfectly recover individual latents. This constitutes, to our knowledge, the first identifiability result for undercomplete nonlinear independent component analysis. Our framework unifies nonlinear ICA, compressed sensing, and neural network interpretability, delineating exactly when representations transition from nonlinear distortions to linear representations and, under additional constraints or steps, to clean, axis-aligned codes. Theoretical predictions are validated on synthetic benchmarks and on activations drawn from vision models, large language models, and macaque inferotemporal cortex.

entry.title: Computational and Statistical Hardness of Calibration Distance

link.title: Computational and Statistical Hardness of Calibration Distance

entry.content:
The distance from calibration, introduced by B{\l}asiok, Gopalan, Hu, and Nakkiran (STOC 2023), has recently emerged as a central measure of miscalibration for probabilistic predictors. We study the fundamental problems of computing and estimating this quantity, given either an exact description of the data distribution or only sample access to it. We give an efficient algorithm that exactly computes the calibration distance when the distribution has a uniform marginal and noiseless labels, which improves the $O(1/\sqrt{|\mathcal{X}|})$ additive approximation of Qiao and Zheng (COLT 2024) for this special case. Perhaps surprisingly, the problem becomes $\mathsf{NP}$-hard when either of the two assumptions is removed. We extend our algorithm to a polynomial-time approximation scheme for the general case. For the estimation problem, we show that $\Theta(1/\epsilon^3)$ samples are sufficient and necessary for the empirical calibration distance to be upper bounded by the true distance plus $\epsilon$. In contrast, a polynomial dependence on the domain size – incurred by the learning-based baseline – is unavoidable for two-sided estimation. Our positive results are based on simple sparsifications of both the distribution and the target predictor, which significantly reduce the search space for computation and lead to stronger concentration for the estimation problem. To prove the hardness results, we introduce new techniques for certifying lower bounds on the calibration distance – a problem that is hard in general due to its $\textsf{co-NP}$-completeness.

entry.title: Conditional Mean Flows: Few-Step Densities for Simulation-Based Inference

link.title: Conditional Mean Flows: Few-Step Densities for Simulation-Based Inference

entry.content:
Flow matching has emerged as a powerful generative family for simulation-based inference (SBI). However, sampling and density evaluation require numerical integration at inference time. This makes posterior sampling in neural posterior estimation costly. More importantly, it can make repeated likelihood evaluation prohibitively expensive and impractical for Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling, which may require thousands of repeated density evaluations. Here, we develop conditional mean flows for posterior and likelihood approximation, combining few-step sampling with tractable density evaluation. We show that the mean flow objective identifies conditional flow maps and that independent masking enables direct estimation of marginal likelihoods. We evaluate both posterior and likelihood estimation across several tasks and show that conditional mean flows retain the flexibility of flow-based density estimators while significantly reducing inference time. In particular, single-step conditional mean flow density evaluation yields estimation error comparable to 200-step flow matching while enabling about 200-fold faster downstream MCMC sampling.

entry.title: Contact, Power, and Balls in Play: A Three-Rate Decomposition of Batting Average and the Disappearance of the .400 Hitter

link.title: Contact, Power, and Balls in Play: A Three-Rate Decomposition of Batting Average and the Disappearance of the .400 Hitter

entry.content:
Batting average factors exactly as BA = c [h + (1-h) b], where c is the rate of avoiding a strikeout, h is the home-run rate among non-strikeout at-bats, and b is batting average on balls in play (BABIP). The bracketed term is the rate f at which non-strikeout at-bats become hits, so the composition nests the two-factor identity BA = c f. Using the 256 major-league hitters with at least 300 at-bats in 2025, every season from 2004 to 2025, and 20,357 qualifying seasons from 1901 to 2019, we ask which rates behave like skills and how the corresponding abilities are related. Over 19 consecutive-season pairs the median year-to-year correlation is 0.86 for c, 0.74 for h and 0.41 for b; batting average (0.44) is no more repeatable than BABIP. A trivariate logistic-normal random-effects model gives single-season reliabilities of 0.91, 0.76 and 0.30, and a talent correlation between contact and power of -0.67 (95% profile interval -0.75 to -0.57), while BABIP talent is only weakly related to either. Historically, the negative covariance between c and f, which was near zero in the dead-ball era, explains why batting averages have become less dispersed, and so why no one has hit .400 since 1941. That covariance runs almost entirely through home runs: removing the contact–power channel from the 2010s covariance recovers 72% of the gap between modern and dead-ball dispersion in batting-average talent.

entry.title: Controlling the False Discovery Rate via Model-Agnostic Importance Measures

link.title: Controlling the False Discovery Rate via Model-Agnostic Importance Measures

entry.content:
Selecting covariates while controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) is critical for interpretable scientific discovery, especially with complex machine learning models. Traditional variable selection methods often rely on specific model assumptions, while Model-X knockoffs provide a general way that leverages knowledge of the covariate distribution to produce a variable selection algorithm. This study puts forward a complementary method to Model-X knockoffs, named Model-Agnostic Selection with agent-X importance (MAS), which utilizes the sample-splitting strategy and a novel variable importance measure to bypass distributional assumptions on covariates. The proposed model-agnostic agent-X importance is defined to evaluate the difference of oracle predictiveness on both the original distribution and the distribution with agent variable in population level, and can be efficiently estimated by constructing the agent variable as some constant and cross-fitting strategy. The MAS method integrates a resplit-per-covariate strategy to decouple estimator dependencies and a data aggregation technique to enhance power. Theoretical guarantees for asymptotic FDR control are established under mild conditions. Extensive simulations and real-data analyses demonstrate that MAS provides competitive performances with existing works in FDR control, computational efficiency and power.

entry.title: Covariance-Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference

link.title: Covariance-Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference

entry.content:
Covariance-calibrated prediction-powered inference (CC-PPI) uses unlabeled prediction scores to calibrate the covariance weight in a GMM estimator. The raw target preserves the prediction-corrected channel and replaces the labeled prediction-covariance contribution in the auxiliary residual metric with its unlabeled counterpart. Spectral protection ensures positive definiteness, and the estimator uses an equal blend of the original covariance and the protected target. We establish first-order efficiency and derive exact finite-sample risk identities for linear regression, including a design-based improvement theorem with tolerance to prediction error. A quadratic decision model gives a midpoint minimax-regret interpretation of the half-strength default. Exact strength-path formulas and convergent risk approximations bound its distance from the best fixed strength on that path. Simulations and four real-data studies show substantial reductions in parameter MSE. Independent fixed-strength references yield only small further gains on the calibration paths studied.

entry.title: Designing Experiments for External Decision Makers

link.title: Designing Experiments for External Decision Makers

entry.content:
Standard Bayesian experimental design (BED) methods assume the experimenter alone will act on the data, choosing the best action given their own beliefs and goals. In practice, data are often acted on by external parties whose procedures the experimenter cannot change and may not know, particularly when the data are released publicly. To extend BED to such settings, we introduce usage-aware experimental design, a framework in which an adaptive design policy is trained to minimise the usage risk: the experimenter’s expected loss when one or more external rules act on the collected data. These rules may be non-Bayesian or black-box, and when several may apply, we either average over them or take the worst case. We show that, unlike in standard BED, more informative data can be harmful under such rules, so the usage risk cannot in general be expressed as an expected uncertainty reduction; our framework thus strictly generalises standard BED. We then use it to tackle a range of problems that are difficult to address with existing approaches.

entry.title: Detectability without Interference: Efficient Canary Design for Privacy Auditing in One Run

link.title: Detectability without Interference: Efficient Canary Design for Privacy Auditing in One Run

entry.content:
Privacy auditing aims to empirically assess privacy leakage in machine learning models using membership inference attacks (MIAs), and to derive lower bounds on differential privacy (DP) parameters. Standard privacy auditing inserts a sensitive sample (a canary) into many ($\gg 100$) randomized training runs, requiring the auditor to detect whether it was included in each run. In one-run auditing, many canaries are included in a single training run, avoiding the high computational cost of multi-run approaches. However, recent theory shows that canaries can interfere with one another, reducing per-canary MIA scores and thereby weakening the audit power. We propose IBIS, a framework that optimizes canaries to maximize their own score while minimizing their impact on others. IBIS combines influence-based greedy initialization with bilevel optimization, introducing a novel regularization term that encourages canaries to be orthogonal in embedding space as a proxy for reducing interference. We propose an efficient bilevel algorithm that incrementally updates a single model at each canary update, avoiding the need to retrain the model from scratch after every update. Experiments show that IBIS offers a better performance-cost trade-off than existing canary crafting approaches, improving MIA metrics while reducing computational cost by up to two orders of magnitude.

link.title: Differentially Private Distribution Release of Gaussian Mixture Models via KL-Divergence Minimization

entry.content:
Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) are widely used statistical models for representing multi-modal data distributions, with numerous applications in data mining, pattern recognition, data simulation, and machine learning. However, recent research has shown that releasing GMM parameters poses significant privacy risks, potentially exposing sensitive information about the underlying data. In this paper, we address the challenge of releasing GMM parameters while ensuring differential privacy (DP) guarantees. Specifically, we focus on the privacy protection of mixture weights, component means, and covariance matrices. We propose to use Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence as a utility metric to assess the accuracy of the released GMM, as it captures the joint impact of noise perturbation on all the model parameters. We develop a KL-divergence-driven optimization framework for differentially private GMM release that jointly designs privacy-budget allocation and parameter perturbations. Through theoretical analysis, we quantify the effects of privacy budget allocation and perturbation statistics on the DP guarantee, and derive a tractable expression for evaluating KL divergence. We formulate and solve an optimization problem to minimize the KL divergence between the released and fitted non-private models, subject to a given $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP constraint. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves strong privacy guarantees while maintaining high utility.

link.title: Diffusion Models in Simulation-Based Inference: A Tutorial Review

entry.content:
Diffusion models have recently emerged as powerful learners for simulation-based inference (SBI), enabling fast and accurate estimation of latent parameters from simulated and real data. Their score-based formulation offers a flexible way to learn conditional or joint distributions over parameters and observations, thereby providing a versatile solution to various modeling problems. We highlight opportunities created by various concepts such as guidance, score composition, flow matching, consistency models, and joint modeling. Furthermore, we discuss how efficiency and statistical accuracy are affected by noise schedules, parameterizations, and samplers. Finally, we illustrate these concepts with case studies across parameter dimensionalities, simulation budgets, and model types, and outline open questions for future research.

entry.title: Dimension-Free PAC-Bayes Generalization for Deep Neural Networks via Dirichlet Processes

link.title: Dimension-Free PAC-Bayes Generalization for Deep Neural Networks via Dirichlet Processes

entry.content:
Classical PAC-Bayesian generalization theory places prior distributions over Euclidean parameter space $\Theta \subseteq \mathbb{R}^D$, causing relative entropy to scale with network dimension $D$. For modern overparameterized neural networks where $D \gg n$, this parameter-counting dependency yields vacuous generalization bounds ($> 1{,}000\%$). In this work, we resolve this barrier by shifting prior specification from internal parameters to the non-parametric space of data distributions $\mathcal{M}_1(\mathcal{Z})$ via a \textbf{Dirichlet Process (DP)}, $\mathcal{DP}(\alpha, F_0)$, inducing parameter distributions through push-forward measures under the learning algorithm. By the Data Processing Inequality, parameter-space relative entropy is strictly bounded by the data-space DP divergence, which we evaluate in exact closed form using Digamma functions. The resulting PAC-Bayesian certificate is strictly invariant to network parameter count $D$, width, and depth. On intrinsic $d^$-dimensional submanifolds, optimal partition scaling achieves the minimax non-parametric rate $\mathcal{O}(n^{-1/(d^+2)} \sqrt{\ln n})$. Across vision architectures scaling up to 4.2 million parameters ($D = 7{,}850$ to $D = 4{,}203{,}522$) on the full MNIST benchmark, while classical weight-space bounds scale past $940\%$ (becoming vacuous), our data-space DP-PAC-Bayes certificate remains stable, non-vacuous, and certified at \textbf{$8.8\%$–$9.4\%$}.

entry.title: Dimension reduction of compositional data through mixtures of latent source compositions

link.title: Dimension reduction of compositional data through mixtures of latent source compositions

entry.content:
Understanding the distribution of mineral compositions is an important challenge in geology. This motivates new variations on dimension reduction for compositional data, lying on a simplex, that approximate observations with lower-dimensional subsimplices. This representation interprets compositions as convex combinations of fewer number of latent source compositions, providing unique insight into the underlying data-generating processes. We develop this approach within the framework of backwards principal component analysis, which constructs nested approximating structures by successive dimension reduction by rank one. We introduce a class of subsimplices, termed proper subsimplices, and provide a formal definition together with a systematic study of their geometric properties. Proper subsimplices admit effective parametrization via hyperplanes, while providing a more flexible approximation than subsimplices obtained by amalgamation. We characterize simple conditions under which hyperplanes generate proper subsimplices. Based on these conditions, we propose both an exact algorithm and a computationally efficient approximate algorithm for estimating proper subsimplex representations. The usefulness of this method is demonstrated on two geochemical datasets where it gives improved insights compared to the conventional PCA approach. Main ideas are further illustrated in a toy example and a simulation study.

entry.title: Diminishing Returns of Data in Sparse Autoencoders: Functional Behavior does not Guarantee Feature Reproducibility

link.title: Diminishing Returns of Data in Sparse Autoencoders: Functional Behavior does not Guarantee Feature Reproducibility

entry.content:
Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are typically trained on hundreds of millions to billions of activation tokens, yet little work has tested whether this scale is necessary. We study how much activation data SAEs need by training four SAE architectures on three language models with budgets ranging from 5M tokens to a 500M-token reference. We measure two notions of convergence: functional behavior on standard evaluations and one-to-one reproducibility of learned features. Functional data requirements are strongly metric-dependent: reconstruction often approaches the full-data reference at substantially smaller budgets, whereas feature reproducibility continues to improve with data. For Gemma-2-2B BatchTopK, the fraction of strictly matched features rises from 2\% at 5M tokens to 29\% at 50M. Data selection also matters: random sampling better preserves the original activation distribution and generally favors reconstruction, whereas diversity-based sampling frequently improves AutoInterp. A theoretical analysis separates statistical consistency of subsampled training from the stronger identifiability and optimization conditions required for one-to-one feature recovery. Our results show that SAE training can often be made far more data-efficient when budgets are matched to the goal, and feature-level claims are backed by explicit reproducibility checks, paving the way toward cheaper and more reliable SAE research.

link.title: Distributionally Robust Regularization of Sparse Integer Programming Trained Learning Models

entry.content:
Building explainable machine learning models is crucial for human users to be able to interpret the proposed statistical relationship obtained from the training data. Mixed-integer optimization formulations are often used to train such models with explicit sparsity constraints, aiming to strike the right trade-off between sparsity and prediction accuracy. Existing methods to find the right choice of sparsity – e.g., via cross-validation – are computationally expensive. For convex model training formulations, recent advances in distributionally robust optimization (DRO) provide strong generalization while sidestepping this computational burden. We describe an extension of such regularization via DRO to mixed-integer sparse programs, providing statistical guarantees as a function of an associated sparsity parameter of the formulation. We illustrate the use of this approach in the case of building explainable binary classification models using sets of feature value rules.

A foundational principle in nonlinear dynamics is that the structure of a dynamical system can be recovered from a small number of generic measurements or coordinates. link.title: Efficient Agnostic Learning of Univariate Densities Under Local Differential Privacy

entry.content:
We propose a general framework for non-interactive locally differentially private (LDP) learning of structured univariate distributions that can be approximated by piece-wise polynomials. This gives the first sample-efficient LDP learners for several distribution classes, including mixtures of log-concave distributions, such as Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). link.title: Efficient GMM and Weighting Matrix under Misspecification

entry.content:
This paper develops efficient GMM estimation under misspecified moment conditions. The influence function of the standard GMM estimator under misspecification depends on both the moment conditions and their Jacobian, motivating a new class of estimators based on augmented, recentered moment conditions. Standard GMM is a special case and generally suboptimal. By optimally weighting the augmented system, we obtain a misspecification-efficient (ME) estimator with the smallest asymptotic variance for the same GMM estimand. In linear models, its asymptotic variance takes the textbook form $(G’W^{}G)^{-1}$, where $W^{}$ is the inverse variance of the residualized moments after projection on the Jacobian $G$. We propose a feasible bootstrap estimator, which is a misspecification-robust and efficient version of the Hall and Horowitz (1996) bootstrap GMM estimator. Finally, we establish uniform local asymptotic minimax bounds over a class of weighting matrices. We illustrate the proposed methods in simulation and two empirical examples.

link.title: Efficiently Computed Marginal Likelihoods for Multivariate Mixture Models

entry.content:
We propose a new methodology for efficiently computing marginal likelihoods for univariate and multivariate mixture models. The estimator that this methodology proposes computes the marginal likelihood from Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samples, is consistent, asymptotically normal and of finite variance. We test it in simulation settings where the true marginal likelihood is available analytically. It performs well against state-of-the-art competitors, even in multivariate settings with a high number of components. We demonstrate its utility for inference and model selection on univariate and multivariate data sets.

entry.content:
Scientists increasingly express their ideas as dynamic models of complex processes. It is often much easier to simulate these models than to calculate the probability of their generating a particular outcome, making likelihood-based estimation infeasible. Existing likelihood-free approaches rely either on manually chosen summary statistics or on representations learned by neural networks. The former is error-prone and laborious, while the latter is computationally intensive, leaving many scientists in a difficult position. We show that, for a large class of dynamic models, parameters can be estimated by matching a small number of random features of the observed and simulated data. In particular, we show that models with a $p$-dimensional parameter can be identified from just $2p+1$ generic random Fourier features. We introduce two estimators for stationary and nonstationary processes, respectively, and we establish their consistency under mild regularity conditions. More broadly, our results serve as the foundation for a new class of methods for simulation-based inference.

Anal., 64 (2026), pp. 1095-1125], we characterize the expected signature kernel of group-valued inhomogeneous L'evy processes, aka L'evy rough paths, as the scalar component of the solution to an extended Goursat-type system. Finally, for conditionally Gaussian martingales, conditioning the usual unbiased empirical squared signature-MMD on the sampled quadratic variations yields an unbiased statistic for the same quantity with no larger variance. We derive computable finite-grid versions and illustrate the resulting variance reduction and gain in power.

entry.content:
We study how to evaluate $K$ target policies simultaneously in stochastic contextual bandits with linear reward structure. Given a known $d$-dimensional feature map and reward-free access to policy queries, we propose PRISMA (Policy evaluation through Regularized Information Sharing and Mixture Allocation), an algorithm that estimates every target policy’s value to accuracy $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$. The algorithm uses $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}!\left( \frac{(L^2S^2+\beta^2)(1\vee\rho^\star)}{\varepsilon^2} \cdot \log(K) \right)$ context draws and reward observations, where $\rho^\star\le d$ is an instance-dependent measure of the difficulty of designing a shared sampling distribution. Here, $L$, $S$, and $\beta$ bound the feature norm, reward parameter norm, and reward noise, respectively, and the suppressed factors are logarithmic in $K$, $d$, and $1/\delta$. Our method combines reward-free planning, a regularized sampling design, and a single ridge regression estimator shared across all target policies. An adaptive doubling procedure selects the regularization scale without knowledge of $\rho^\star$. The guarantees require no numerical lower bound on second-moment eigenvalues and have no explicit dependence on the cardinalities of the context and action spaces. Policy-query costs are accounted for separately, with $K$ queries per shared planning context.

entry.content:

entry.title: Failure Is the Mother of Success: Recovering Supervision with Grounding Hindsight

link.title: Failure Is the Mother of Success: Recovering Supervision with Grounding Hindsight

entry.content:
When every rollout for a problem fails, GRPO receives neither a successful exemplar nor a nonzero group-relative advantage, so it learns nothing from exactly the problems it most needs to learn. The policy writes a corrective note about each failed attempt without seeing a reference answer or solution, then re-solves the problem with the note in context. Because admission is decided by fresh successes rather than by the failed rollout itself, the procedure can recover supervision from groups in which every attempt failed, and it applies equally to failures in mixed groups. Only the policy is trained, the only judge is the outcome verifier, and deployment requires no notes or extra inference. Across model families and sizes and two training domains, RSHD consistently improves over GRPO on in-domain benchmarks, and the gains carry over to out-of-domain evaluation sets.

link.title: Finite-History Outage Certification for Partially Observed Fluid Antenna Receivers

entry.content:
Fluid antenna receivers can select a service position from partial port observations, but finite historical data leave uncertainty in the covariance used for that decision. We develop deployment-before-use reliability certification for a frozen partial-observation rule. A proper predictive density defines a history-based parameter region. Gaussian covariance envelopes, shared conditional-probability bounds and selector enclosures provide simultaneous risk bounds over continuous parameters and discontinuous port decisions. Separate history-coverage and integration budgets limit erroneous positive certification to 0.05 for a single qualification procedure under the stated stationary model and numerical assumptions. A separate coupled comparison gives a current-rule outage interval of $[7.6820,9.1266]\times10^{-4}$ and resolves lower outage than two observed-port controls using the same historical fit. One independently recalibrated history reuses the certificate without additional risk sampling. Unresolved and adverse-member controls delimit this reuse.

entry.title: Flexible Doubly Robust Proximal Causal Inference for Censored Outcomes

link.title: Flexible Doubly Robust Proximal Causal Inference for Censored Outcomes

entry.content:
Estimating causal effects on right-censored time-to-event outcomes is challenging under unmeasured confounding. Proximal causal inference addresses unmeasured confounding through proxy variables, but existing proximal survival methods rely largely on restrictive parametric bridge models. We introduce Proximal Survival Bridge learning (PSB), a flexible doubly robust proximal framework for censored outcomes. Building on existing proximal identification of treatment-specific survival curves, the framework yields outcome-bridge (OB), treatment-bridge (TB), and doubly robust (DR) estimators, with two flexible bridge learners: PSB-K, a kernel estimator with a low-rank time decomposition, and PSB-N, a neural estimator trained by a projected maximum-moment-restriction loss. Unlike existing flexible proximal learners for scalar outcomes, PSB directly handles censoring and survival-curve targets. On a standard SEM benchmark, a proximal semi-synthetic ACTG study, and the real-world Framingham study, PSB-K performs strongest on SEM and ACTG, whereas PSB-N is the most stable on Framingham. Additional results with modern causal survival baselines, weakened or invalid proxies, and heavier censoring assess robustness across challenging settings.
